lead: A jet engine cannot light its fuel at standstill: the compressor gives no airflow until something turns it. A starter spins the high-pressure spool until there is enough air for combustion; then ignition and fuel take over and the engine accelerates to idle on its own. Only a few universities teach this topic in detail, but the starting circuit, the exciter and the start sequence are classic exam questions.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for bleed air used by air starters, and Chapter 2.4 for the fuel that must be lit.

blocks.text: A starter is a motor that turns the HP compressor through the accessory gearbox. It supplies torque until the engine is well past self-sustaining speed, the N2 at which the engine can keep turning without help (N2 is HP spool speed as a percentage of its rated speed). The starter is cut out by N2, not by a clock.

An air turbine starter (ATS) is a small turbine driven by regulated bleed air. A start valve admits air from the APU, a running engine (cross-bleed start) or a ground cart. A reduction gear and an overrunning clutch drive the gearbox; at cut-out the start valve closes and the clutch lets the running engine overrun the starter, so the engine cannot overspeed it.

An electric starter is a DC series motor, chosen because it gives its highest torque at zero speed. On turboprops, helicopters and APUs it is often a starter-generator: one machine cranks the engine on 28 V DC and then becomes the DC generator. Large turbofans use air starters because an electric motor of the same power would be far too heavy.

The electrical start circuit keeps a light start switch away from the starter’s current, which can reach several hundred amperes. The start switch energises a start relay; its heavy contacts (the starter contactor) connect the battery or ground power to the motor. A current limiter or a resistance in series softens the first surge, and a time relay or an N2 speed switch opens the contactor at cut-out. The same relay logic energises the ignition relay, so the exciters work only during the start.

An ignition exciter takes 28 V DC or 115 V AC and charges a storage capacitor to a few kilovolts. When the capacitor voltage reaches the breakdown of a sealed discharge gap, the stored energy is dumped into the igniter plug, a spark gap in the combustor liner, as one intense spark; most exciters give one or two sparks a second. The energy in each spark is set by the capacitor:

blocks.where: E is the stored energy in joules (J), C is the capacitance in farads (F) and V is the charging voltage in volts (V).

blocks.text: Spark energies run from a few joules to about 20 J. The higher energy is used for starting and relight, because a cold, fast-moving mixture is hard to light; the lower energy is used for continuous ignition in flight, in heavy rain, turbulence, icing or on contaminated runways, so a flameout relights at once; it saves plug life. Two exciters and two plugs give redundancy. Piston engines are different: a magneto, an engine-driven generator with its own coil and contact breaker, makes the spark for each cylinder, and every engine has two magnetos.

In an automatic start the FADEC runs the sequence. The values below are those of one common narrow-body auto-start (an A320-family aircraft with CFM56-5B engines); other engines use other numbers, so quote them only from that engine’s start schedule.

items: START is selected; the start valve opens and the starter cranks N2.
At about 16 % N2 the igniters are energised.
At about 22 % N2 the HP fuel valve opens; light-off follows within seconds and EGT rises.
Starter and combustion together accelerate the spool; at about 50 % N2 the start valve closes and the ignition switches off.
The engine accelerates to idle, near 60 % N2, on its own.

blocks.text: Interlocks stop unsafe starts: the start valve will not open with low bleed pressure, fuel is inhibited below a minimum N2, and the igniters are on before fuel arrives, so fuel lights as soon as it enters. Early ignition is harmless; early or excess fuel is not.

items: Hot start: EGT passes the start limit, from too much fuel for the airflow (weak starter, tailwind, early fuel). Cut fuel at once.
Hung start: light-off occurs but N2 stops rising below idle, from low starter air or a weak battery. Abort before EGT climbs.
Wet start (no light-off): fuel enters but does not light. Cut fuel, then dry-motor (crank with fuel and ignition off) to clear it.

spec.aria: Graph of N2 in percent against time in seconds. A line rises from zero to 22 percent at 13.75 seconds, then more steeply to 50 percent at 25.4 seconds, then dashed to idle near 60 percent. Markers: ignition at 16 percent and 10 seconds, fuel at 22 percent and 13.75 seconds, starter cut-out at 50 percent and 25.4 seconds. Side panel: a 4 microfarad capacitor at 2 kilovolts stores 8 joules.

examples.question: During an auto-start N2 rises at a steady 1.6 % per second while only the starter turns the engine. After light-off, starter and combustion together raise N2 at 2.4 % per second. Ignition comes on at 16 % N2, fuel at 22 % N2 (take light-off as immediate) and the starter cuts out at 50 % N2. Find the time of each event from the start of cranking.
steps: From 22 % to 50 % at 2.4 % per second takes (50 − 22) ÷ 2.4 = 11.67 s.
Check the order: 10.0 s < 13.75 s < 25.4 s, so the igniters are already sparking when fuel arrives.
examples.answer: Ignition at 10.0 s, fuel and light-off at 13.75 s, starter cut-out at 25.4 s after cranking began.

examples.question: An exciter has a 4.0 µF storage capacitor charged to 2.0 kV and fires one spark per second. Find the energy per spark and the average output power. What charging voltage would give a 20 J spark with the same capacitor?
steps: Power = energy per spark × sparks per second = 8.0 J × 1 s⁻¹ = 8.0 W.
examples.answer: 8.0 J per spark, 8.0 W on average; about 3.16 kV gives a 20 J spark.

traps: N1 is fan speed; the start schedule runs on N2, the HP spool.
A hot start is an EGT exceedance; a hung start is N2 stopping below idle after light-off; a wet start has no light-off at all.
Cut-out is triggered by N2, not by clock time, and it comes well above self-sustaining speed.
Early or excess fuel causes a hot start. Ignition must be on before fuel, so early ignition is correct, not a fault.
Spark energy goes with V², not V: doubling the capacitor voltage gives four times the energy.

quiz.a: The N2 above which the engine keeps turning without starter help.

quiz.q: Why is fuel admitted after ignition and only above a minimum N2?
quiz.a: Above the minimum N2 there is enough airflow for a mixture that is not too rich; with the igniters already sparking, the fuel lights as soon as it arrives, so it cannot collect and cause a hot start.

quiz.q: A start reaches 72 % N2 in 24 s. Find the average acceleration.
A 2.0 µF capacitor is charged to 3.0 kV. Find the spark energy.
EGT rises fast towards the limit just after light-off while N2 is rising slowly. Name the event and the first action.
quiz.a: A developing hot start: too much fuel for the airflow. Cut the fuel at once, keep the starter turning (dry motoring) to blow out the fuel and cool the engine, and record the peak EGT.

quiz.q: Name the two common starter types.
quiz.a: The air turbine starter and the electric (DC series) starter or starter-generator.

quiz.q: Why does a starter circuit use a relay or contactor instead of passing current through the start switch?
quiz.a: The starter draws several hundred amperes. A small cockpit switch energises a relay whose heavy contacts carry that current, so the switch and its wiring stay light and do not burn.

quiz.q: A cross-bleed start lights off but hangs at 40 % N2. Give two likely causes.
quiz.a: Low starter air (the other engine at too low a power, a duct leak or a start valve not fully open), or a weak starter or high accessory load; the engine has fuel and fire but not enough help to reach idle.

beyond: Not for the exam. FADEC auto-start watches N2, EGT and fuel flow and aborts hot, hung and wet starts by itself. Starter-generators are growing in more-electric aircraft: the Boeing 787 starts its engines with its generators run as motors. Health monitoring records start times and EGT peaks to predict starter and igniter wear.
